claims.claim: The most common autoimmune condition in the HTP cohort is AITD, affecting 53.1% of the total cohort.
claims.source: In this analysis, the most common autoimmune condition is AITD, affecting 53.1% of the total cohort (Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1a, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the HTP cohort analysis, supported by data in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: Autoimmune and inflammatory skin conditions represent the second most common category in the HTP cohort, affecting 43% of the cohort.
claims.source: Grouped together, autoimmune and inflammatory skin conditions represent the second most common category, affecting 43% of the cohort, including: atopic dermatitis / eczema (27.9%), hidradenitis suppurativa / folliculitis / boils (20.6%), alopecia areata (7.7%), psoriasis (6.1%), and vitiligo (1.9%; Figure 1a, Figure 1—figure supplement 1b, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding from the HTP cohort analysis, supported by data in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: The rate of celiac disease in the HTP cohort is 9.6%, which is highly elevated over that of the general population.
claims.source: The rate of celiac disease (9.6%) is also highly elevated over that of the general population (Singh et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the HTP cohort analysis with a citation for comparison to the general population.

claims.claim: 10 cases (2.2%) of juvenile Type I diabetes were observed in the HTP cohort.
claims.source: We observed 10 cases (2.2%) of juvenile Type I diabetes, which has been reported to be more common in DS (Aitken et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the HTP cohort analysis with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Analysis of age trajectories of immune-related conditions in DS revealed early onset, with >80% of AITD, autoimmune/inflammatory skin conditions, and celiac disease being diagnosed in the first two decades of life.
claims.source: Within the HTP cohort, analysis of age trajectories of immune-related conditions in DS revealed early onset, with >80% of AITD, autoimmune/inflammatory skin conditions, and celiac disease being diagnosed in the first two decades of life (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–e).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the HTP cohort analysis, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c–e.

claims.claim: The cumulative burden of autoimmunity and autoinflammation is similar in males versus females with DS, albeit with slightly increased rates of AITD and hidradenitis suppurativa in females.
claims.source: The cumulative burden of autoimmunity and autoinflammation is similar in males versus females with DS, albeit with slightly increased rates of AITD and hidradenitis suppurativa in females (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the HTP cohort analysis, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claims.claim: 75% of adult participants with DS had a history of at least one autoimmune/inflammatory condition (AITD, autoimmune/inflammatory skin conditions, or celiac disease).
claims.source: In terms of co-occurrence, when evaluating the adult population (18+years old) for AITD, autoimmune/inflammatory skin conditions and celiac disease, we found that 75% of participants had a history of at least one condition, 38.4% had at least two, and 13.6% had three or more conditions (Figure 1b, Figure 1—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the HTP cohort analysis, supported by data in Figure 1b.

claims.claim: 82.4% of adults with DS show positivity for anti-TPO or ANA, with 41.2% being positive for both.
claims.source: Remarkably, 82.4% of adults with DS show positivity for at least one of these autoantibodies, with 41.2% being positive for both (Figure 1c, Figure 1—source data 2).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from autoantibody measurements in the HTP cohort, supported by data in Figure 1c.

claims.claim: 62% of individuals with history of hypothyroidism were TPO+.
claims.source: Indeed, 62% of individuals with history of hypothyroidism were TPO+, whereby anti-TPO is just one of the possible autoantibodies associated with AITD.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from autoantibody measurements in the HTP cohort.

claims.claim: 25 autoantibodies are significantly over-represented in people with DS relative to age- and sex-matched controls.
claims.source: These efforts identified 25 autoantibodies significantly over-represented in people with DS relative to age- and sex-matched controls (Figure 1d), with 98.3% of individuals with DS being positive for at least one of these autoantibodies, and 63.3% being positive for six or more (Figure 1d–e).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from autoantibody profiling using protein array technology, supported by data in Figure 1d.

claims.claim: 98.3% of individuals with DS are positive for at least one of the 25 autoantibodies over-represented in DS.
claims.source: These efforts identified 25 autoantibodies significantly over-represented in people with DS relative to age- and sex-matched controls (Figure 1d), with 98.3% of individuals with DS being positive for at least one of these autoantibodies, and 63.3% being positive for six or more (Figure 1d–e).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from autoantibody profiling, supported by data in Figure 1d-e.

claims.claim: Individuals with hypothyroidism are more likely to be positive for anti-TPO antibodies.
claims.source: Expectedly, individuals with hypothyroidism are more likely to be positive for anti-TPO antibodies (Figure 1g–h).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analysis of autoantibody positivity relative to co-occurring conditions, supported by data in Figure 1g-h.

claims.claim: TPO+ status associates with higher rates of use of pressure equalizing (PE) tubes employed to alleviate the symptoms of recurrent ear infections and otitis media with effusion (OME).
claims.source: However, unexpectedly, TPO+ status also associates with higher rates of use of pressure equalizing (PE) tubes employed to alleviate the symptoms of recurrent ear infections and otitis media with effusion (OME), which is common in DS (Elling et al., 2023, Figure 1g–h).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analysis of autoantibody positivity relative to co-occurring conditions, supported by data in Figure 1g-h.

claims.claim: Positivity for additional autoantibodies was more common in those with other co-occurring neurological conditions.
claims.source: Positivity for additional autoantibodies was more common in those with other co-occurring neurological conditions, a broad classification encompassing various seizure disorders, movement disorders, and structural brain abnormalities (Figure 1g–h, Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analysis of autoantibody positivity relative to co-occurring conditions, supported by data in Figure 1g-h.

claims.claim: Individuals with history of tricuspid valve regurgitation display higher rates of four different autoantibodies, most prominently against WARS1 and SRP68.
claims.source: Individuals with history of tricuspid valve regurgitation display higher rates of four different autoantibodies, most prominently against WARS1, a tryptophan tRNA synthetase mutated in various neurodevelopmental disorders (Lin et al., 2022), and SRP68, a protein commonly targeted by autoantibodies in necrotizing myopathies (Allenbach et al., 2020, Figure 1—figure supplement 1g).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analysis of autoantibody positivity relative to co-occurring conditions, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1g.

claims.claim: Individuals with a history of frequent pneumonia present a higher frequency of autoantibodies against DSG3 (desmoglein 3).
claims.source: Individuals with a history of frequent pneumonia present a higher frequency of autoantibodies against DSG3 (desmoglein 3), a cell adhesion molecule targeted by autoantibodies in paraneoplastic pemphigus (PNP), an autoimmune disease of the skin and mucous membranes that can involve fatal lung complications (Amagai et al., 1998, Figure 1g–h).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analysis of autoantibody positivity relative to co-occurring conditions, supported by data in Figure 1g-h.

claims.claim: Massive immune remodeling occurs in all major myeloid and lymphoid subsets in DS, including increases in basophils, along with depletion of eosinophils and total B cells.
claims.source: In agreement with previous analyses (Waugh et al., 2019; Araya et al., 2019; Lambert et al., 2022; Galbraith et al., 2023; Malle et al., 2023), we observed massive immune remodeling in all major myeloid and lymphoid subsets, including increases in basophils, along with depletion of eosinophils and total B cells (Figure 2a-c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a-c).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from mass cytometry analysis, supported by data in Figure 2a-c and previous citations.

claims.claim: Global immune changes in DS are largely independent of the presence of clinical diagnoses or autoantibody positivity.
claims.source: When comparing various subgroups within the DS cohort based on autoimmunity status, we observed that these global immune changes are largely independent of the presence of clinical diagnoses or autoantibody positivity, with very few additional changes significantly associated with these measures of autoimmunity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from mass cytometry analysis comparing subgroups, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claims.claim: The significant depletion of B cells and enrichment of basophils in DS is not significantly different among various autoimmunity subgroups.
claims.source: For example, the significant depletion of B cells and enrichment of basophils in DS is not significantly different among the various subgroups (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from mass cytometry analysis comparing subgroups, supported by data in Figure 2c.

claims.claim: Non-classical monocytes are further elevated in the ANA+ group.
claims.source: Among CD45+ CD66lo non-granulocytes, most changes are conserved among subgroups, with the sole of exception of non-classical monocytes, which are further elevated in the ANA+ group (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d–e).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from mass cytometry analysis comparing subgroups, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d-e.

claims.claim: γδ T cells (both total and CD8+) are depleted in those with multiple autoimmune diagnoses.
claims.source: Notably, we observed depletion of γδ T cells (both total and CD8+) in those with multiple autoimmune diagnoses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d,f), a result that is in line with reports documenting depletion of these subsets from peripheral circulation toward sites of active autoimmunity (Amini et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from mass cytometry analysis comparing subgroups, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1d,f and a citation.

claims.claim: Age-associated B cells (ABCs) tend to be further elevated in the TPO+ group.
claims.source: Among B cells, the overall shift toward more differentiated states such as plasmablasts, age-associated B cells (ABCs), and IgM+ memory cells is also conserved among subgroups, with the sole exception of ABCs, which tend to be further elevated in the TPO+ group (Figure 2g–i, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d,g).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from mass cytometry analysis comparing subgroups, supported by data in Figure 2g-i.

claims.claim: T21 causes global remodeling of the immune system toward an autoimmunity-prone and pro-inflammatory state, prior to clinically evident autoimmunity.
claims.source: Altogether, these results indicate that T21 causes global remodeling of the immune system toward an autoimmunity-prone and pro-inflammatory state, prior to clinically evident autoimmunity, and dwarfing any additional effects associated with confirmed diagnoses of autoimmune/inflammatory conditions or common biomarkers of autoimmunity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mass cytometry analysis results.

claims.claim: Individuals with DS display elevated levels of many inflammatory markers, including several interleukins, cytokines, and chemokines known to drive autoimmune conditions, such as IL-6 and TNF-α.
claims.source: It is well established that individuals with DS display elevated levels of many inflammatory markers, including several interleukins, cytokines, and chemokines known to drive autoimmune conditions, such as IL-6 and TNF-α (Sullivan et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017; Malle et al., 2023; Galbraith et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is stated as well-established knowledge with supporting citations.

claims.claim: Profound hypercytokinemia occurs in DS, with significant elevation of multiple acute phase proteins, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and chemokines.
claims.source: These efforts confirmed the notion of profound hypercytokinemia in DS (Sullivan et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2017; Malle et al., 2023; Galbraith et al., 2023), with significant elevation of multiple acute phase proteins (e.g. CRP, SAA, IL1RA), pro-inflammatory cytokines (TSLP, IL-17C, IL-22, IL-17D, IL-9, IL-6, TNF-α) and chemokines (IP-10, MIP-3a, MIP-1a, MCP-1, MCP-4, Eotaxin), as well as growth factors associated with inflammation and wound healing (FGF, PIGF, VEGF-A; Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from plasma proteomics analysis, supported by data in Figure 3a and previous citations.

claims.claim: No important differences in inflammatory markers were observed within the DS cohort based on various metrics of autoimmunity (number of autoimmune/inflammatory conditions, ANA or TPO positivity status, or number of other autoantibodies).
claims.source: However, when evaluating for differences within the DS cohort based on various metrics of autoimmunity, we did not observe important differences based on number of autoimmune/inflammatory conditions, ANA or TPO positivity status, or number of other autoantibodies (Figure 3a).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from plasma proteomics analysis comparing subgroups, supported by data in Figure 3a.

claims.claim: CRP, IL-6, and TNF-α are equally elevated across all autoimmunity subgroups in DS.
claims.source: For example, CRP, IL-6, and TNF-α are equally elevated across all these subgroups (Figure 3b–d, Figure 3—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from plasma proteomics analysis comparing subgroups, supported by data in Figure 3b-d.

claims.claim: Many inflammatory factors elevated in DS across the lifespan do not display a significant increase with age, such as IL-9 and IL-17C.
claims.source: We then compared the effects of age versus T21 status on cytokine levels in the DS cohort, which identified many inflammatory factors elevated in DS across the lifespan that do not display a significant increase with age, such as IL-9 and IL-17C, or that increase with age only in the DS cohort, such as IP-10 (Figure 3e–f, Figure 3—figure supplement 1e).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from analysis of age effects on cytokine levels, supported by data in Figure 3e-f.

claims.claim: T21 induces a constitutive hypercytokinemia from early childhood, with only a fraction of these inflammatory changes being exacerbated with age.
claims.source: Altogether, these results indicate that T21 induces a constitutive hypercytokinemia from early childhood, with only a fraction of these inflammatory changes being exacerbated with age.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the plasma proteomics and age analysis results.

claims.claim: IFN hyperactivity and downstream JAK/STAT signaling are key drivers of immune dysregulation in DS.
claims.source: Several lines of evidence support the notion that IFN hyperactivity and downstream JAK/STAT signaling are key drivers of immune dysregulation in DS (Sullivan et al., 2016; Sullivan et al., 2017; Waugh et al., 2019; Araya et al., 2019; Powers et al., 2019; Tuttle et al., 2020; Chi et al., 2023; Galbraith et al., 2023; Waugh et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is stated as a conclusion supported by multiple citations.

claims.claim: In mouse models of DS, both normalization of IFNR gene copy number and pharmacologic JAK1 inhibition rescue their lethal immune hypersensitivity phenotypes.
claims.source: In mouse models of DS, both normalization of IFNR gene copy number and pharmacologic JAK1 inhibition rescue their lethal immune hypersensitivity phenotypes (Tuttle et al., 2020; Waugh et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: IFN transcriptional scores derived from peripheral immune cells correlate significantly with the degree of immune remodeling and hypercytokinemia in DS.
claims.source: Furthermore, we recently demonstrated that IFN transcriptional scores derived from peripheral immune cells correlate significantly with the degree of immune remodeling and hypercytokinemia in DS (Galbraith et al., 2023), and we and others have reported the safe use of JAK inhibitors for treatment of diverse immune conditions in DS, including alopecia areata (Rachubinski et al., 2019), psoriatic arthritis (Pham et al., 2021) and hemophagocytic lymphohistocytosis (Guild et al., 2022) through small case series.
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: No adverse events were observed that required a change or cessation of tofacitinib dosing in the first 10 participants.
claims.source: This analysis established that there were no AEs that required a change or cessation of tofacitinib dosing and that this medicine is well tolerated in individuals with DS.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis.

claims.claim: Tofacitinib is well tolerated in individuals with DS.
claims.source: This analysis established that there were no AEs that required a change or cessation of tofacitinib dosing and that this medicine is well tolerated in individuals with DS.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the interim clinical trial analysis.

claims.claim: Seven of the ten participants had an improvement in the IGA score.
claims.source: The interim analysis showed that seven of the ten participants had an improvement in the IGA score and eight of the ten reported some improvement on their life quality related to their skin condition as measured by the DLQI (Figure 5a-b, Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis, supported by data in Figure 5a-b.

claims.claim: Eight of the ten participants reported some improvement on their life quality related to their skin condition as measured by the DLQI.
claims.source: The interim analysis showed that seven of the ten participants had an improvement in the IGA score and eight of the ten reported some improvement on their life quality related to their skin condition as measured by the DLQI (Figure 5a-b, Figure 5—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis, supported by data in Figure 5a-b.

claims.claim: Five of six participants with alopecia areata showed scalp hair regrowth.
claims.source: The most striking effects were observed for alopecia areata (Figure 5c-d, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a). Five of six participants with alopecia areata showed scalp hair regrowth, with the exception being a male participant (AA1) with history of alopecia totalis for 20+years who only showed facial hair and eyelash re-growth.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis, supported by data in Figure 5c-d.

claims.claim: One participant with psoriasis due to psoriatic arthritis experienced an almost complete remission of psoriatic arthritis symptoms.
claims.source: One participant presented with psoriasis due to psoriatic arthritis and experienced an almost complete remission of psoriatic arthritis symptoms (Ps1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b–c).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis, supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b-c.

claims.claim: For the two participants that presented with atopic dermatitis, the clinical manifestations were markedly reduced during tofacitinib treatment.
claims.source: For the two participants that presented with atopic dermatitis, the clinical manifestations were markedly reduced during tofacitinib treatment (Figure 5e–f).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis, supported by data in Figure 5e-f.

claims.claim: At baseline, clinical trial participants show IFN scores within the typical range for DS, but values are decreased at 2, 8, and 16 weeks of tofacitinib treatment.
claims.source: At baseline, clinical trial participants show IFN scores within the typical range for DS, but values are decreased at 2, 8, and 16 weeks of tofacitinib treatment (Figure 6a, Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis, supported by data in Figure 6a.

claims.claim: Most participants show a decrease in IFN scores as soon as two weeks of treatment which is sustained over time.
claims.source: Time course analysis revealed that most participants show a decrease in IFN scores as soon as two weeks of treatment which is sustained over time, with two clear exceptions (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis, supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claims.claim: ISGs as a group are significantly downregulated upon tofacitinib treatment, but the effect is not uniform across all ISGs.
claims.source: Collectively, ISGs as a group are significantly downregulated upon tofacitinib treatment, but the effect is not uniform across all ISGs (Figure 6c), indicating that JAK1/3 inhibition does not reduce all IFN signaling elevated in DS, which could be explained by the fact that the IFN pathways also employ JAK2 for signal transduction (Schwartz et al., 2016; Schwartz et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis, supported by data in Figure 6c and citations.

claims.claim: Tofacitinib treatment reverses the dysregulation of many gene signatures observed in DS, effectively attenuating many pro-inflammatory signatures beyond IFN gamma and alpha responses.
claims.source: Global analysis of transcriptome changes revealed that tofacitinib treatment reverses the dysregulation of many gene signatures observed in DS, effectively attenuating many pro-inflammatory signatures beyond IFN gamma and alpha responses, such as Inflammatory Response, TNF-α signaling via NFkB, IL-2 STAT5 signaling, and IL-6 JAK STAT3 signaling (Figure 6—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis, supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: At baseline, clinical trial participants show cytokine scores within the range observed for DS, but these values decrease at 2, 8 and 16 weeks relative to baseline.
claims.source: At baseline, clinical trial participants show cytokine scores within the range observed for DS, but these values decrease at 2, 8 and 16 weeks relative to baseline (Figure 6d–e, Figure 6—figure supplement 1e, Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis, supported by data in Figure 6d-e.

claims.claim: The decreases in TNF-α and IL-6 observed upon tofacitinib treatment indicate that elevation of these potent inflammatory cytokines requires sustained JAK/STAT signaling in DS.
claims.source: The decreases in TNF-α and IL-6 observed upon tofacitinib treatment indicate that elevation of these potent inflammatory cytokines requires sustained JAK/STAT signaling in DS (Figure 6e).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the clinical trial results, supported by data in Figure 6e.

claims.claim: Seven of the 10 participants presented at baseline with anti-TPO levels above the upper limit of normal (ULN, 60 U/mL), and all seven experienced a decrease in these auto-antibodies at 8 weeks and 16 weeks relative to baseline.
claims.source: Seven of the 10 participants presented at baseline with anti-TPO levels above the upper limit of normal (ULN, 60 U/mL), and all seven experienced a decrease in these auto-antibodies at 8 weeks and 16 weeks relative to baseline (Figure 6f, Figure 6—source data 1).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis, supported by data in Figure 6f.

claims.claim: For one participant (HS1) anti-TPO levels decreased below the ULN while on the trial.
claims.source: In fact, for one participant (HS1) the levels decreased below the ULN while on the trial.
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis.

claims.claim: Three participants had anti-TG levels above the ULN (4 IU/mL) and all three showed a decrease from baseline levels while on tofacitinib at both 8 and 16 weeks.
claims.source: Additionally, three of these seven participants also had anti-TG levels above the ULN (4 IU/mL) and all three showed a decrease from baseline levels while on tofacitinib at both 8 and 16 weeks, with one participant (AA6) falling below the ULN upon treatment (Figure 6f).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis, supported by data in Figure 6f.

claims.claim: Tofacitinib treatment lowers IFN scores and cytokine levels to within the range observed in the general population, not below, indicating that this immunomodulatory strategy can provide therapeutic benefit in DS without overt immune suppression.
claims.source: Importantly, tofacitinib treatment lowers IFN scores and cytokine levels to within the range observed in the general population, not below, indicating that this immunomodulatory strategy can provide therapeutic benefit in DS without overt immune suppression.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the clinical trial results.

claims.claim: During treatment, both IFN scores and cytokine scores remain sensitive to immune stimuli, as evidenced by participants who had received a vaccine or experienced an URI before a blood draw.
claims.source: Importantly, during treatment, both IFN scores and cytokine scores remain sensitive to immune stimuli, as evidenced by participants who had received a vaccine or experienced an URI before a blood draw (Figure 6a, Figure 6—figure supplement 1f).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from the interim clinical trial analysis, supported by data in Figure 6a and Figure 6—figure supplement 1f.

claims.claim: The fact that levels of IL-6 and TNF-α are reduced upon tofacitinib treatment supports the use of JAK inhibitors over TNF-blockers or anti-IL-6 agents in this population.
claims.source: Importantly, the fact that levels of IL-6 and TNF-α are reduced upon tofacitinib treatment supports the use of JAK inhibitors over TNF-blockers or anti-IL-6 agents in this population.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the clinical trial results.

claims.claim: The clear decrease in anti-TPO and anti-TG levels indicates that autoreactive B cell function requires elevated JAK/STAT signaling.
claims.source: The clear decrease in anti-TPO and anti-TG levels indicates that autoreactive B cell function requires elevated JAK/STAT signaling, but whether this effect is cell-autonomous versus a consequence of a reduced systemic inflammatory milieu will require further investigation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the clinical trial results.

claims.claim: Gene signatures of IFN hyperactivity are present in human embryonic tissues with T21.
claims.source: The fact that gene signatures of IFN hyperactivity are present in human embryonic tissues with T21 (Bhattacharya et al., 2023) and embryonic tissues from mouse models of DS (Aziz et al., 2018; Waugh et al., 2023) indicates that the harmful effects of IFN hyperactivity could start in utero, supporting the notion that DS could be understood, in part, as an inborn error of immunity with similarities to monogenic interferonopathies (Rodero and Crow, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is stated with supporting citations.

claims.claim: The harmful effects of IFN hyperactivity could start in utero in DS.
claims.source: The fact that gene signatures of IFN hyperactivity are present in human embryonic tissues with T21 (Bhattacharya et al., 2023) and embryonic tissues from mouse models of DS (Aziz et al., 2018; Waugh et al., 2023) indicates that the harmful effects of IFN hyperactivity could start in utero, supporting the notion that DS could be understood, in part, as an inborn error of immunity with similarities to monogenic interferonopathies (Rodero and Crow, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on cited evidence.

claims.claim: DS could be understood, in part, as an inborn error of immunity with similarities to monogenic interferonopathies.
claims.source: The fact that gene signatures of IFN hyperactivity are present in human embryonic tissues with T21 (Bhattacharya et al., 2023) and embryonic tissues from mouse models of DS (Aziz et al., 2018; Waugh et al., 2023) indicates that the harmful effects of IFN hyperactivity could start in utero, supporting the notion that DS could be understood, in part, as an inborn error of immunity with similarities to monogenic interferonopathies (Rodero and Crow, 2016).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on cited evidence.

claims.claim: T21 causes widespread multi-organ autoimmunity of pediatric onset, with production of autoantibodies targeting every major organ system.
claims.source: Results presented here demonstrate that T21 causes widespread multi-organ autoimmunity of pediatric onset, with production of autoantibodies targeting every major organ system.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the discussion based on the results presented.

claims.claim: Elevated levels of anti-TPO in individuals with history of use of ear tubes suggests an interplay between otitis media and endocrine dysfunction in DS.
claims.source: Elevated levels of anti-TPO in individuals with history of use of ear tubes suggests an interplay between otitis media and endocrine dysfunction in DS (Koçyiğit et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the results with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: It is possible that recurrent ear infections cause a chronic immune stimulus that lead to eventual breach of tolerance in this autoimmunity-prone population, even perhaps through epitope mimicry.
claims.source: For example, it is possible that recurrent ear infections cause a chronic immune stimulus that lead to eventual breach of tolerance in this autoimmunity-prone population, even perhaps through epitope mimicry (Ercolini and Miller, 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the results with a supporting citation.

claims.claim: Elevation of SRP68 autoantibodies in DS suggests a potential autoimmune basis for musculoskeletal and cardiovascular complications in DS.
claims.source: Elevation of SRP68 autoantibodies in DS (Figure 1d and f), which are common in necrotizing myopathies with cardiovascular involvement (Allenbach et al., 2020), suggests a potential autoimmune basis for musculoskeletal and cardiovascular complications in DS, which also warrants additional research.

results.result: Down syndrome (DS), caused by trisomy 21 (T21), is characterized by immune dysregulation including increased interferon responses, JAK/STAT signaling, elevated autoantibodies, global immune remodeling, and hypercytokinemia, along with various developmental and clinical features.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C5 and C14-C17 establish well-documented background knowledge about DS based on prior literature. These claims are supported by multiple citations and represent established knowledge in the field, providing appropriate context for the current study.

results.result: Prior work from the authors and others demonstrates that T21 causes interferon hyperactivity and JAK/STAT signaling dysregulation, with evidence from mouse models showing that normalization of IFNR gene copy number or JAK inhibition rescues multiple DS phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C27 summarize prior work with appropriate citations. These establish the rationale for the current study by demonstrating that IFN hyperactivity is a key feature of DS and that JAK inhibition shows promise in mouse models. The claims are well-supported by cited literature.

results.result: Analysis of 441 individuals with DS in the HTP cohort reveals high prevalence of autoimmune conditions, with AITD affecting 53.1%, autoimmune/inflammatory skin conditions affecting 43%, celiac disease at 9.6%, and early onset with >80% diagnosed in the first two decades of life.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C34 present descriptive epidemiological findings from the HTP cohort with clear sample sizes (n=441) and are supported by Figure 1 data. The findings are internally consistent and provide quantitative characterization of autoimmune burden in DS across the lifespan.

results.result: Autoantibody profiling reveals that 82.4% of adults with DS are positive for anti-TPO or ANA, and 98.3% are positive for at least one of 25 autoantibodies significantly over-represented in DS compared to controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 present findings from autoantibody measurements with clear methodology (protein array technology, n=120 T21, n=60 D21 controls) and statistical testing (Fisher's exact test with FDR correction). The high prevalence of autoantibodies is well-documented in Figure 1 and represents a major finding.

results.result: Specific autoantibodies show unexpected associations with clinical phenotypes in DS, including TPO+ status associating with PE tube use, and elevated autoantibodies in individuals with neurological conditions, tricuspid valve regurgitation, and frequent pneumonia.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C43 report associations between autoantibodies and clinical conditions. While the statistical associations are documented (Figure 1g-h), the biological interpretation and causality remain unclear. The unexpected association between anti-TPO and PE tube use (C40) is particularly speculative. Sample sizes for some subgroups may be limited, and multiple testing concerns exist.

results.result: Mass cytometry analysis reveals massive immune remodeling in DS affecting all major immune cell subsets, with these changes being largely independent of clinical autoimmune diagnoses or autoantibody positivity, indicating T21 causes constitutive immune dysregulation prior to clinically evident autoimmunity.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C50 present findings from mass cytometry analysis (n=292 T21, n=96 controls) with appropriate statistical methods (beta regression with FDR correction). The key finding that immune changes precede clinical autoimmunity is well-supported by subgroup comparisons showing minimal differences based on autoimmunity status (Figure 2). This represents a major conceptual advance.

results.result: Plasma proteomics reveals profound hypercytokinemia in DS with elevation of multiple inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, TNF-α, etc.) that is constitutive from early childhood and largely independent of autoimmunity status, with only a fraction of changes exacerbated with age.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C56 present findings from plasma proteomics analysis (54 markers, n=346 T21, n=131 controls) using appropriate statistical methods (linear regression with FDR correction). The finding that hypercytokinemia precedes clinical autoimmunity and is distinct from age-related changes is well-supported by Figure 3 data and represents an important mechanistic insight.

results.result: Multiple lines of evidence support that IFN hyperactivity and JAK/STAT signaling are key drivers of immune dysregulation in DS, with mouse models and prior human studies demonstrating the therapeutic potential of JAK inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 synthesize prior evidence with appropriate citations to establish the rationale for JAK inhibition. These claims appropriately distinguish between established findings from mouse models (C58) and correlative human data (C59), providing sound justification for the clinical trial.

results.result: Interim analysis of the first 10 participants completing 16 weeks of tofacitinib treatment (5 mg twice daily) shows good safety profile with no serious adverse events requiring treatment cessation, demonstrating that tofacitinib is well tolerated in individuals with DS.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C60-C61 report safety outcomes from the clinical trial with clear documentation of adverse events (Figure 4). The sample size (n=10) is appropriate for an interim safety analysis. However, the conclusion of 'well tolerated' should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample size and short duration (16 weeks). Longer-term safety data are needed.

results.result: Tofacitinib treatment improved skin pathology across multiple conditions, with 7/10 participants showing IGA improvement, 8/10 reporting improved quality of life (DLQI), and particularly striking effects in alopecia areata (5/6 showing scalp hair regrowth).
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C62-C66 report clinical improvements from the trial (Figure 5). While the descriptive results are clearly documented, the lack of statistical testing (per interim analysis plan), absence of a control group, small sample size (n=10), and potential for placebo effects limit the strength of conclusions. The improvements are suggestive but require confirmation in the full trial with appropriate statistical analysis.

results.result: Tofacitinib treatment decreased IFN scores at 2, 8, and 16 weeks, with most participants showing sustained decreases. ISGs as a group were significantly downregulated, though effects were not uniform across all ISGs, and treatment reversed dysregulation of multiple pro-inflammatory gene signatures.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C67-C70 report molecular outcomes from the trial with appropriate statistical testing (paired Wilcox tests) and comparison to the HTP cohort (Figure 6a-c). The finding that IFN scores decrease but remain sensitive to immune stimuli (vaccines, infections) is well-documented. The gene-specific effects of tofacitinib are appropriately characterized with mechanistic interpretation regarding JAK1/3 vs JAK2 signaling.

results.result: Tofacitinib treatment decreased cytokine scores at 2, 8, and 16 weeks, with significant reductions in TNF-α and IL-6, indicating that elevation of these inflammatory cytokines requires sustained JAK/STAT signaling in DS.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C71-C72 report cytokine outcomes with appropriate statistical testing and comparison to the HTP cohort (Figure 6d-e). The mechanistic interpretation that TNF-α and IL-6 elevation requires sustained JAK/STAT signaling (C72) is reasonable given the observed decreases, though causality cannot be definitively established from this intervention study alone.

results.result: Tofacitinib treatment decreased levels of pathogenic autoantibodies, with all 7 participants with elevated anti-TPO showing decreases at 8 and 16 weeks, and all 3 with elevated anti-TG showing decreases, indicating that autoreactive B cell function requires elevated JAK/STAT signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C73-C75, C79 report autoantibody outcomes with clear documentation (Figure 6f). The consistent decreases in anti-TPO and anti-TG across all affected participants is compelling. However, the mechanistic interpretation (C79) that this reflects B cell-autonomous effects vs. systemic inflammation is appropriately acknowledged as uncertain and requiring further investigation.

results.result: JAK inhibition is a valid strategy to treat autoimmune conditions in DS, as tofacitinib normalizes IFN scores and cytokine levels to within the range of the general population without overt immune suppression, while maintaining sensitivity to immune stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C13, C76-C78 present broad conclusions about JAK inhibition as a therapeutic strategy. While the interim data are encouraging, the small sample size (n=10), lack of control group, short duration (16 weeks), and absence of formal statistical testing for the primary endpoint limit the strength of this conclusion. The claim that this approach avoids 'overt immune suppression' (C76) is supported by the observation that immune responses remain intact, but longer-term safety data are needed.

results.result: T21 causes widespread multi-organ autoimmunity of pediatric onset with production of autoantibodies targeting every major organ system, occurring concurrently with constitutive immune remodeling and hypercytokinemia from an early age prior to autoimmune diagnoses or autoantibody production.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C7, C83 synthesize the major findings from the HTP cohort analysis. These conclusions are well-supported by the comprehensive data on autoimmune conditions (Figure 1), immune cell profiling (Figure 2), and cytokine analysis (Figure 3). The temporal relationship showing immune dysregulation precedes clinical autoimmunity is a key conceptual advance supported by the data.

results.result: Gene signatures of IFN hyperactivity are present in human and mouse embryonic tissues with T21, suggesting harmful effects could start in utero and supporting the notion that DS could be understood as an inborn error of immunity with similarities to monogenic interferonopathies.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 synthesize findings from cited literature to propose a conceptual framework. The presence of IFN signatures in embryonic tissues (C80) is well-supported by citations. The interpretation that effects begin in utero (C81) and the comparison to interferonopathies (C82) are reasonable inferences from the cited evidence, though appropriately presented as speculative ('could be understood').

results.result: Specific autoantibody-phenotype associations suggest potential autoimmune mechanisms for various DS complications, including an interplay between otitis media and endocrine dysfunction, and autoimmune contributions to musculoskeletal and cardiovascular complications.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 present speculative interpretations of the autoantibody findings. While the associations are documented, the mechanistic interpretations (epitope mimicry in C85, autoimmune basis for complications in C86) are highly speculative and appropriately acknowledged as requiring additional research. These represent hypothesis-generating observations rather than established findings.

results.result: Measurements of specific immune cell types or cytokines in the bloodstream are unlikely to provide diagnostic value for autoimmunity in DS, given the constitutive immune changes regardless of autoimmunity status.
results.evaluation: Claim C87 presents a reasonable conclusion based on the finding that immune changes are largely independent of clinical autoimmunity status (Figures 2-3). This negative finding has important implications for clinical practice and biomarker development in DS.

results.result: JAK1 inhibitors are the most logical choice to dampen IFNR gene triplication effects, and tofacitinib shows gene-specific effects that attenuate IFN and cytokine scores to general population levels while preserving some inflammatory processes and immune activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C90 present mechanistic rationale and interpretation of the trial results. The rationale for JAK1 inhibition (C88) is sound based on IFNR signaling biology. The observations about gene-specific effects (C90) and normalization without over-suppression (C89) are well-supported by the transcriptome and cytokine data (Figure 6).

results.result: The study characterizes the prevalence and early onset of autoimmune conditions in a large DS cohort (n=441), finding that AITD affects 53.1%, skin conditions affect 43%, celiac disease affects 9.6%, and >80% of these conditions are diagnosed in the first two decades of life, with 75% of adults having at least one autoimmune condition.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised this work as 'compelling, comprehensive, and state-of-the-art clinical, immunological, and autoantibody assessment' and 'an unparalleled examination of immune disorder in a large number of patients with DS.' The large cohort size and systematic evaluation were highlighted as major strengths, with one reviewer noting 'the number of patients (and controls) utilized for this study is remarkable and allows to draw much firmer conclusions.'

results.result: The study demonstrates widespread autoantibody production in DS, with 82.4% of adults positive for anti-TPO or ANA, 98.3% positive for at least one of 25 autoantibodies over-represented in DS, and 63.3% positive for six or more autoantibodies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers recognized this as a novel contribution, with one stating the work 'extend[s] these observations to highlight early-onset immunological aberrancies, far before symptoms occur, as well as characterizing novel autoantibody reactivities in this patient population.' The comprehensive autoantibody profiling was acknowledged as providing 'new insights into the immune phenotype of patients with DS.'

results.result: The study identifies unexpected autoantibody-phenotype associations in DS, including associations between TPO+ status and ear tube use, autoantibodies and neurological conditions, WARS1/SRP68 antibodies and tricuspid valve regurgitation, and DSG3 antibodies and frequent pneumonia.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged these findings as part of the 'unexpected autoantibody-phenotype associations' that represent a major advance. One reviewer noted the work provides 'new insights into the immune phenotype of patients with DS,' implicitly accepting these novel associations. No reviewer challenged the validity of these correlations.

results.result: Mass cytometry analysis reveals massive immune remodeling in DS (including basophil enrichment, B cell depletion, and shifts in T cell and B cell subsets) that is largely independent of autoimmune diagnoses or autoantibody status, indicating T21 causes constitutive immune dysregulation prior to clinical autoimmunity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly supported this finding, with one noting 'it is interesting that regardless of autoimmune disease or autoantibody status, individuals with DS have elevated cytokines and CRP.' Another reviewer acknowledged the work demonstrates 'immune dysregulation is present from infancy.' One reviewer noted that 'several of the alteration reported in this manuscript had already been suggested' but emphasized the large cohort 'allows to draw much firmer conclusions.'

results.result: Plasma proteomics demonstrates profound hypercytokinemia in DS with elevation of acute phase proteins, pro-inflammatory cytokines, and chemokines that is independent of autoimmunity status and present from early childhood, with some cytokines (IL-9, IL-17C) elevated across the lifespan without age-related increases.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirmed this result, with one stating 'it is interesting that regardless of autoimmune disease or autoantibody status, individuals with DS have elevated cytokines and CRP' and noting 'some cytokines are significant elevated in people with DS starting in infancy (e.g., IL-9 and IL-17C).' The early onset and independence from disease state were recognized as important findings.

results.result: Interim analysis of 10 participants completing 16 weeks of tofacitinib treatment shows good safety profile with no serious adverse events requiring dosing changes, and the treatment is well tolerated in individuals with DS.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly supported the safety findings, with one stating 'the treatment is tolerated without serious adverse effects' and another noting 'the early results support that treatment is well tolerated.' The editor described the results as 'promising results from a clinical trial with the JAK inhibitor tofacitinib.' No safety concerns were raised by any reviewer.

results.result: Tofacitinib treatment reduced skin pathology across multiple conditions (alopecia areata, psoriasis, atopic dermatitis), with 7/10 participants showing IGA improvement, 8/10 reporting quality of life improvement, and particularly striking effects in alopecia areata (5/6 showing scalp hair regrowth).
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the clinical efficacy, with one stating 'the majority of patients have experienced clinical improvement or remission in their corresponding clinical cutaneous manifestations.' Another noted 'Most patients experienced clinical improvement, with alopecia areata having the greatest response.' The variable response across conditions was acknowledged, with one reviewer noting 'Treatment may not affect all skin disease equally, for example of the 5 patients with hidradenitis suppurativa, only 1 showed clinical improvement.'

results.result: Tofacitinib treatment decreased interferon scores and cytokine scores at 2, 8, and 16 weeks, with most participants showing sustained decreases in IFN scores from two weeks onward, and global transcriptome analysis revealing reversal of multiple pro-inflammatory gene signatures beyond IFN responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly supported these immunological outcomes, with one stating the treatment led to 'improvement or normalization of aberrant immunological signals such as cytokines' and another noting 'improvement of interferon scores in patients.' The comprehensive molecular characterization was recognized as part of the 'state-of-the-art' assessment.

results.result: Tofacitinib treatment decreased levels of pathogenic autoantibodies, with all 7 participants having elevated anti-TPO at baseline showing decreases at 8 and 16 weeks, one participant's anti-TPO falling below the upper limit of normal, and similar decreases observed for anti-TG antibodies.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirmed the autoantibody reduction, with one stating the treatment led to 'reduction of autoantibodies.' The finding was recognized as part of the overall positive immunological outcomes. No reviewer questioned the validity or significance of the autoantibody decreases.

results.result: Tofacitinib treatment lowers IFN scores and cytokine levels to within the range of the general population (not below), and immune responses remain sensitive to stimuli (vaccines, infections), indicating therapeutic benefit without overt immune suppression.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly recognized this important safety consideration, with one noting the treatment provides 'therapeutic benefit in DS without overt immune suppression.' The preservation of immune responsiveness was implicitly accepted as no reviewer raised concerns about immunosuppression despite the small sample size and short follow-up.

results.result: The study concludes that JAK inhibition is a valid therapeutic strategy for autoimmune conditions in DS, with the reduction of IL-6 and TNF-α supporting the use of JAK inhibitors over TNF-blockers or anti-IL-6 agents in this population.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the 'promising' interim results and that the trial is 'a critically important step for the field,' they also emphasized limitations. One reviewer noted 'the clinical trial results reported here are preliminary and based on interim analysis of 10 patients at 16 weeks' and stated 'it is unclear how long therapy, if of benefit, would need to be continued.' Another acknowledged 'the relatively small size of tofacitinib-treated DS patients' as an inherent weakness. The conclusion is supported by early data but requires longer-term validation.

results.result: Background claims establishing that DS is caused by trisomy 21, involves immune dysregulation including increased IFN responses, JAK/STAT signaling, autoantibodies, and hypercytokinemia, and that mouse models support the role of IFN receptors and JAK inhibition in DS phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these background claims without challenge. One reviewer explicitly stated 'Prior studies from these authors and others have convincingly demonstrated that individuals with DS have immune dysregulation including increased Type I IFN activity, elevated production of inflammatory cytokines (hypercytokinemia), increased autoantibodies, and populations of dysregulated adaptive immune cells.' The established nature of these findings was not questioned.

results.result: Background claims establishing that IFN hyperactivity and JAK/STAT signaling are key drivers of immune dysregulation in DS, supported by mouse model data and correlations between IFN scores and immune phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these mechanistic background claims as established, with one noting 'Prior studies from these authors and others have convincingly demonstrated' the role of IFN dysregulation. The rationale for JAK inhibition was not challenged by any reviewer.

results.result: Mechanistic interpretations that TNF-α and IL-6 elevation requires sustained JAK/STAT signaling and that autoreactive B cell function requires elevated JAK/STAT signaling, based on the observed decreases with tofacitinib treatment.
results.evaluation: Reviewers implicitly accepted these mechanistic interpretations by not challenging them and by affirming the overall immunological outcomes. The interpretations are logical extensions of the observed treatment effects and align with the reviewers' positive assessment of the results.

results.result: Discussion and speculative claims about DS as an inborn error of immunity, potential in utero effects of IFN hyperactivity, mechanisms linking autoantibodies to clinical phenotypes, diagnostic implications, and the specificity of tofacitinib effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these interpretive and speculative claims. One reviewer explicitly stated 'The authors appropriately acknowledge areas that require more research and areas that are not well understood,' indicating acceptance of the speculative nature of some conclusions. The discussion was implicitly accepted as reasonable given the data presented.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on epidemiological findings from HTP cohort (C28-C34). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes methodological rigor and sample size, while peer reviewers praise the work as 'compelling, comprehensive, and state-of-the-art' with 'remarkable' patient numbers.

Perfect agreement on autoantibody findings (C35-C38). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights clear methodology and statistical testing, while peer reviewers recognize this as novel contribution providing 'new insights into the immune phenotype of patients with DS.'

Disagreement on autoantibody-phenotype associations (C39-C43). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN citing speculative interpretations and multiple testing concerns, while peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, acknowledging these as 'unexpected' but valid novel associations without challenging their validity.

Perfect agreement on mass cytometry findings (C44-C50). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the conceptual advance that immune changes precede clinical autoimmunity, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm this finding as 'interesting' and note it allows 'much firmer conclusions.'

Strong agreement on plasma proteomics findings (C51-C56). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval covers C51-C56, peer review focuses on C52-C56. Both emphasize that hypercytokinemia precedes clinical autoimmunity and is present from infancy, with peer reviewers noting specific cytokines like IL-9 and IL-17C.

Perfect agreement on trial safety outcomes (C8, C60-C61). Both evaluations rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate documentation but cautions about small sample size and short duration, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm treatment is 'well tolerated' without raising safety concerns.

Perfect agreement on clinical improvement claims (C9, C62-C66). Both rate as SUPPORTED, though OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN. OpenEval emphasizes limitations (no control group, small n=10, no statistical testing), while peer reviewers affirm clinical efficacy and acknowledge variable response across conditions.

Strong agreement on molecular outcomes (C10, C67-C70 in OpenEval; C10, C11, C67-C71 in peer review). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes appropriate statistical testing and mechanistic interpretation, while peer reviewers affirm 'improvement or normalization of aberrant immunological signals.'

Strong agreement on autoantibody reduction (C12, C73-C75 overlap). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes compelling consistent decreases but acknowledges mechanistic uncertainty (C79), while peer reviewers affirm reduction as part of positive immunological outcomes without questioning validity.

Perfect agreement on JAK inhibition rationale (C57-C59). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate distinction between mouse models and human correlative data, while peer reviewers accept these mechanistic background claims as established without challenge.

Strong agreement on background claims about DS (C1-C5, C14-C17 in OpenEval overlap with C1-C5, C14-C26 in peer review). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes well-documented background with multiple citations, while peer reviewers explicitly state prior studies have 'convincingly demonstrated' these findings.

Strong agreement on IFN hyperactivity background (C18-C26 overlap). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate citations establishing study rationale, while peer reviewers accept these as established findings from prior work without challenge.

Agreement on overall therapeutic conclusion (C13, C76-C78) but different confidence levels. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN citing small sample size and short duration, while peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN but more positively, calling results 'promising' while acknowledging they are 'preliminary' and require longer-term validation.

OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, emphasizing highly speculative nature as hypothesis-generating, while peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting speculative claims as reasonable given the data and acknowledging authors' appropriate caveats.
